title: Legg–Calvé–Perthes Disease

content_blocks.text: Spontaneous deterioration of the femoral head and neck, leading to an incongruent, malformed coxofemoral joint and secondary osteoarthritis.
Precise cause unknown; a specific vascular lesion not identified.
Histologic evidence points to infarction of vessels supplying the proximal femur.
Necrosis of subchondral bone leads to collapse of subchondral bone and deformation of the femoral head during normal loading.
Articular cartilage becomes thickened, develops clefts, and undergoes superficial fraying.
Simultaneous osseous degeneration and repair is characteristic of ischemia and revascularization of bone.
No known association with hypercoagulability or other coagulopathy.
Musculoskeletal—causes a pelvic limb lameness; insidious in onset.
Manchester terriers have multifactorial inheritance pattern with a high degree of heritability.
Probable autosomal recessive inheritance in miniature poodles, West Highland white terriers, Yorkshire terriers, and pugs.
Most common among adolescent dogs of miniature, toy, and small breeds.
Toy breeds and terriers are most susceptible.

FHNE or micro THR—treatment of choice.
Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs)—preoperative or postoperative; minimize joint pain; reduce synovitis; reduce soft tissue pain and inflammation to encourage postsurgery limb use:
Carprofen 2.2 mg/kg PO q12h or 4.4 mg/kg PO q24h.
Grapiprant 2 mg/kg PO q24h, to animals >3.6 kg.
Meloxicam—load 0.2 mg/kg PO, then 0.1 mg/kg PO q24h—liquid.
NSAIDs—gastrointestinal disease, liver disease, or renal disease may preclude use in some patients.

NSAIDs—can cause gastrointestinal tract ulceration, hepatotoxicity, or nephrotoxicity; inhibition of platelet activity may increase hemorrhage at surgery; discontinue aspirin for at least 1 week before surgery, if possible.
NSAIDs—do not use in conjunction with glucocorticoids; risk of gastrointestinal tract ulceration; consider appropriate wash-out times when switching from one NSAID to another.

Chondroprotective drugs (e.g., polysulfated glycosaminoglycans, glucosamine, and chondroitin sulfate)—minimal benefit in advanced disease; no evidence to suggest that these drugs prevent or reverse the disease process.
Postsurgical progress checks—1- to 2-week intervals depending on progress with limb use; ensure compliance with exercise recommendations.
Conservative therapy—reevaluate after 4–6 weeks of strict rest (physical examination, radiographs) to determine if surgery is needed.
Do not repeat dam–sire breeding that resulted in affected offspring.
Noncompliance with postsurgical physical therapy exercises may result in less than optimal limb function.
FHNE—good to excellent prognosis for full recovery (84–100% success rate).
Micro THR—excellent prognosis for full recovery.
Conservative therapy—reported to alleviate lameness after 2–3 months in less than 25% of patients.
Usually affects juvenile small-breed dogs, but mature dogs may be affected by chronic disease.
